children.name: Fregata
children.description: The sole genus of the family, comprising five species of large, lightly built seabirds instantly recognisable by their deeply forked tails, long hooked bills, and the male's inflatable red throat pouch. Frigatebirds are masters of aerial piracy, harrying other seabirds to force them to disgorge their catch.

children.name: Fregata magnificens
children.description: The magnificent frigatebird, frigate petrel or man o' war is a seabird of the frigatebird family Fregatidae. With a length of 89–114 centimetres and wingspan of 2.17–2.44 m, it is the largest species of frigatebird. It occurs over tropical and subtropical waters off America, between northern Mexico and Peru on the Pacific coast and between Florida and southern Brazil along the Atlantic coast.

children.name: Fregata minor
children.description: The great frigatebird (Fregata minor) is a large seabird in the frigatebird family.

children.name: Fregata ariel
children.description: thumb| Egg of Fregata ariel - [[MHNT]] The lesser frigatebird (Fregata ariel) is a seabird of the frigatebird family Fregatidae.

children.name: Fregata aquila
children.description: The Ascension frigatebird (Fregata aquila) is a seabird of the frigatebird family Fregatidae which breeds on Boatswain Bird Island and Ascension Island in the tropical Atlantic Ocean.

children.name: Fregata andrewsi
children.description: The Christmas frigatebird (Fregata andrewsi) or Christmas Island frigatebird is a seabird of the frigatebird family Fregatidae which is an endemic breeder to Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean.

children.name: Anhinga
children.description: The sole genus of the family, containing four species of slender, snake-necked waterbirds found across warm freshwaters worldwide. Unlike most waterbirds, darters lack waterproof feathers and must spread their wings to dry after each fishing foray, a familiar sight along tropical waterways.

children.name: Anhinga melanogaster
children.description: The Oriental darter (Anhinga melanogaster) is a water bird of tropical South Asia and Southeast Asia.

children.name: Anhinga rufa
children.description: The African darter (Anhinga rufa), sometimes called the snakebird, is a water bird of Sub-Saharan Africa and Iraq.

children.name: Anhinga novaehollandiae
children.description: The Australasian darter or Australian darter (Anhinga novaehollandiae) is a species of bird in the darter family, Anhingidae.

children.name: Microcarbo
children.description: Pygmy cormorants — small, long-tailed cormorants of freshwater lakes and rivers in Africa, southern Asia, and Australasia. The smallest members of the cormorant family, they have proportionally longer tails and shorter bills than their larger relatives. Pygmy cormorants are highly gregarious, often nesting in mixed colonies with herons and ibises, and they employ a cooperative feeding strategy where groups drive fish into shallows before diving.

children.name: Microcarbo pygmaeus
children.description: The pygmy cormorant (Microcarbo pygmaeus) is a member of the Phalacrocoracidae (cormorant) family of seabirds.

children.name: Microcarbo africanus
children.description: The reed cormorant (Microcarbo africanus), also known as the long-tailed cormorant, is a bird in the cormorant family Phalacrocoracidae.

children.name: Microcarbo coronatus
children.description: The crowned cormorant (Microcarbo coronatus) or , is a small cormorant that is endemic to the waters of the cold Benguela Current of southern Africa.

children.name: Microcarbo niger
children.description: The little cormorant (Microcarbo niger) is a member of the cormorant family of seabirds.

children.name: Microcarbo melanoleucos
children.description: The little pied cormorant, little shag or little pied shag (Microcarbo melanoleucos) ( ) is a common species of Australasian waterbird, found around the coasts, islands, estuaries, and inland waters of Australia, New Guinea, New Zealand, Timor-Leste and Indonesia, and around the islands of the south-western Pacific and the subantarctic.

children.name: Poikilocarbo
children.description: Red-legged cormorant — a monotypic genus found along the Pacific coast of South America from northern Peru to Tierra del Fuego. Easily distinguished from all other cormorants by its vivid coral-red legs and feet, which contrast sharply with its grey-blue plumage and orange throat patch. The red-legged cormorant is a specialist of exposed rocky shores and strong tidal currents, where it forages in the surf zone among breaking waves.

children.name: Urile
children.description: North Pacific cormorants — a genus of four species that breed on the cold coasts and islands of the northern Pacific Rim, from Japan and Kamchatka across the Aleutians to western North America. They have distinctive bare facial skin patterns and, in most species, a bright blue or purple gape. One species, the spectacled cormorant, is the only cormorant to have gone extinct in historical times, vanishing from the Commander Islands around 1850.

children.name: Urile pelagicus
children.description: The pelagic cormorant (Urile pelagicus), also known as Baird's cormorant or violet-green cormorant, is a small member of the cormorant family Phalacrocoracidae.

children.name: Urile perspicillatus
children.description: The spectacled cormorant or Pallas's cormorant (Urile perspicillatus) is an extinct marine bird of the cormorant family of seabirds that inhabited Bering Island and possibly other places in the Commander Islands and the nearby coast of Kamchatka in the far northeast of Russia.

children.name: Phalacrocorax
children.description: Great cormorants and shags — large, fish-eating waterbirds whose distinctive habit of spreading their wings to dry after diving is one of the most familiar sights at coasts and inland waters worldwide. Cormorants lack the fully waterproofed plumage of ducks and grebes, instead using partially water-permeable feathers that reduce buoyancy and help them pursue fish at depth — but require post-dive drying. This genus includes the most widespread and familiar cormorant species found across every continent except South America, ranging from the world's largest cormorant colony to species restricted to single island groups.

children.name: Phalacrocorax neglectus
children.description: The bank cormorant (Phalacrocorax neglectus), also known as Wahlberg's cormorant, is a medium-sized cormorant that is endemic to Namibia and the western seaboard of South Africa, living in and around coastal waters; it is rarely recorded more than 15 km offshore.

children.name: Phalacrocorax nigrogularis
children.description: The Socotra cormorant (Phalacrocorax nigrogularis) is a threatened species of cormorant that is endemic to the Persian Gulf and the south-east coast of the Arabian Peninsula.

children.name: Phalacrocorax featherstoni
children.description: The Pitt shag (Phalacrocorax featherstoni), also known as the Pitt Island shag or Featherstone's shag, is a species of bird in the family Phalacrocoracidae.

children.name: Phalacrocorax punctatus
children.description: The spotted shag or pārekareka (Phalacrocorax punctatus) is a species of cormorant endemic to New Zealand.

children.name: Phalacrocorax varius
children.description: The Australian pied cormorant (Phalacrocorax varius), also known as the pied cormorant, pied shag, or great pied cormorant, is a medium-sized member of the cormorant family.

children.name: Phalacrocorax fuscicollis
children.description: The Indian cormorant or Indian shag (Phalacrocorax fuscicollis) is a member of the cormorant family.

children.name: Phalacrocorax capensis
children.description: The Cape cormorant, also known as the Cape shag, is a member of the cormorant family. It is endemic to the southwestern coast of Africa, and classified as "Endangered" by the IUCN. The Cape cormorant is most closely related to the great cormorant and Japanese cormorant.

children.name: Phalacrocorax capillatus
children.description: The Japanese cormorant (Phalacrocorax capillatus), also known as Temminck's cormorant, is a species of cormorant native to coastal areas of the east Palearctic.

children.name: Phalacrocorax carbo
children.description: The great cormorant, also known as just cormorant in Britain, as black shag or kawau in New Zealand, formerly also known as the great black cormorant across the Northern Hemisphere, the black cormorant in Australia, and the large cormorant in India, is a widespread member of the cormorant family of seabirds. It breeds in much of the Old World, Australasia, and the Atlantic coast of North America.

children.name: Gulosus
children.description: European shag — a monotypic genus separated from Phalacrocorax by molecular studies, restricted to the temperate and boreal coastal waters of Europe and North Africa. The European shag is distinguished from the great cormorant by its smaller size, more slender build, iridescent green-black plumage, and a distinctive forward-curling crest in breeding plumage. Unlike the great cormorant, it is strictly a marine species that rarely if ever ventures onto fresh water.

children.name: Gulosus aristotelis
children.description: The European shag or common shag (Gulosus aristotelis) is a species of cormorant.

children.name: Nannopterum
children.description: American cormorants — a genus of three species restricted to the Americas, including the only flightless cormorant in the world. These cormorants have undergone rapid evolutionary diversification in the New World, from the Galápagos flightless cormorant to the widespread double-crested and neotropic cormorants. The genus was long lumped into Phalacrocorax but molecular studies confirm its distinctness, with the flightless cormorant representing an extreme adaptation to an island environment without terrestrial predators.

children.name: Nannopterum harrisi
children.description: The flightless cormorant (Nannopterum harrisi), also known as the Galápagos cormorant, is a cormorant endemic to the Galápagos Islands, and an example of the highly unusual fauna there.

children.name: Nannopterum brasilianum
children.description: | range_map_caption = Range of Nannopterum brasilianum.

children.name: Leucocarbo
children.description: Blue-eyed shags — a southern-hemisphere genus of medium to large cormorants found around the Antarctic and subantarctic islands, the southern coasts of South America, and New Zealand. They are named for the vivid blue ring around the eye that most species display, a feature unique among cormorants. Many Leucocarbo species have extremely restricted ranges, confined to single island groups, making them among the most range-restricted of all seabirds and particularly vulnerable to introduced predators.

children.name: Leucocarbo magellanicus
children.description: | image2 = | image2_caption = Puñihuil, Ancud, Chiloé Island, Chile | genus = Leucocarbo | species = magellanicus | authority = (Gmelin, 1789) | synonyms = * Phalacrocorax magellanicus * Notocarbo magellanicus | range_map = Phalacrocorax magellanicus map.svg | range_map_caption =.

children.name: Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum
children.description: The guanay cormorant or guanay shag (Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum) is a member of the cormorant family found on the Pacific coast of Peru and northern Chile.

children.name: Leucocarbo ranfurlyi
children.description: The Bounty shag (Leucocarbo ranfurlyi), also known as the Bounty Island shag, is a species of cormorant of the family Phalacrocoracidae.

children.name: Leucocarbo colensoi
children.description: The Auckland shag or Auckland Islands shag (Leucocarbo colensoi) is a species of cormorant from New Zealand.

children.name: Leucocarbo campbelli
children.description: The Campbell shag (Leucocarbo campbelli), also known as the Campbell Island shag, is a species of bird in the family Phalacrocoracidae.
children.namedAfter: Campbell Island (named after Captain John Campbell)

children.name: Leucocarbo atriceps
children.description: The imperial shag or imperial cormorant (Leucocarbo atriceps) is a black-and-white cormorant native to southern South America, islands of the Subantarctic, and the Antarctic Peninsula, primarily in rocky coastal regions, but locally also at large inland lakes.

children.name: Leucocarbo melanogenis
children.description: The Crozet shag (Leucocarbo melanogenis), also known as the South Georgia cormorant, is a marine cormorant native to the Crozet, Prince Edward and Marion islands in the South Atlantic Ocean.

children.name: Leucocarbo bransfieldensis
children.description: The Antarctic shag (Leucocarbo bransfieldensis), sometimes referred to as the imperial cormorant, king cormorant, imperial shag, blue-eyed shag or Antarctic cormorant, is the only species of the cormorant family found in the Antarctic.

children.name: Leucocarbo verrucosus
children.description: The Kerguelen shag (Leucocarbo verrucosus) is a species of cormorant endemic to the Kerguelen Islands in the southern Indian Ocean, one of the most isolated places on Earth.

children.name: Leucocarbo purpurascens
children.description: The Macquarie shag (Leucocarbo purpurascens), Macquarie Island shag or Macquarie Island cormorant, is a marine cormorant native to Macquarie Island in the Southern Ocean, about halfway between Australia and Antarctica.

children.name: Morus
children.description: Europe's largest seabird, plunge-diving from 30 metres at 100 km/h, closing its wings at the last moment. Air sacs beneath the skin and around the skull cushion the impact. Thousands pass along the Swedish west coast in autumn heading to Atlantic wintering areas.

children.name: Morus bassanus
children.description: The Northern gannet is a seabird, the largest species of the gannet family, Sulidae. It is native to the coasts of the North Atlantic Ocean, breeding in Western Europe and Northeastern North America. It is the largest seabird in the northern Atlantic.

children.name: Morus capensis
children.description: The Cape gannet (Morus capensis) is a large seabird of the gannet family, Sulidae.

children.name: Morus serrator
children.description: The Australasian gannet (Morus serrator), also known as the Australian gannet or tākapu, is a large seabird of the booby and gannet family, Sulidae.

children.name: Sula dactylatra
children.description: The masked booby (Sula dactylatra), also called the masked gannet or the blue-faced booby, is a large seabird of the booby and gannet family, Sulidae.

children.name: Sula granti
children.description: The Nazca booby (Sula granti) is a large seabird of the booby family, Sulidae, native to the eastern Pacific.

children.name: Sula variegata
children.description: The Peruvian booby (Sula variegata) is an endemic bird of the Peruvian current, and an important predator of the marine community to which it belongs.

children.name: Sula leucogaster
children.description: The brown booby (Sula leucogaster) is a large seabird in the booby and gannet family Sulidae, of which it is one of the most common and widespread species.
